screens.title: Why DNS and NTP Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the failure modes. DNS resolves human-friendly hostnames to IP addresses. If DNS fails, services that rely on names cannot connect and many automation tools break when they cannot reach package mirrors or A P I endpoints. A concrete example is a web server configured to reach a backend by hostname; if resolv. conf points to incorrect servers or network rules block DNS, the web server fails to reach the backend even though network connectivity may exist. NTP prevents clock drift. If a server's clock drifts, authentication protocols and certificate validity checks can fail. For example, Kerberos authentication and TLS certificate validation both depend on reasonably synchronized clocks. A practical contrast: editing /etc/resolv. conf manually can appear to work for a single session, but NetworkManager may overwrite the file when interfaces change. The recommended practice is to set DNS in the NetworkManager connection profile using community. general. nmcli so the setting persists and is associated with a named interface. For NTP, modern RHEL uses chrony instead of ntpd; deploy a templated chrony. conf so every host points to approved NTP sources. In short: persistent, automated configuration avoids intermittent failures and simplifies troubleshooting. Ask yourself: if a host cannot resolve names or has a wrong time, which user-facing services would fail first in your environment?

Concrete Example

screens.title: DNS on RHEL and NetworkManager
screens.narratorSegment: On RHEL systems NetworkManager commonly manages network interfaces and the contents of the file /etc/resolv. conf. That file lists the DNS servers and search domains the resolver uses. If you edit that file directly, NetworkManager or an interface event can overwrite your changes. The more robust pattern is to declare DNS servers on the NetworkManager connection profile itself so the DNS configuration is bound to an interface name like System eth0. The community. general. nmcli Ansible module lets you express connection-level DNS settings in a reproducible way. For example, set dns4 to a list such as 192.168.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 and set dns4_search to include example. com. When applied, NetworkManager updates its profile and applies the settings, which persist and survive reboots and reactivations. A common misconception is that using ansible. builtin. template on /etc/resolv. conf is sufficient; while possible, it risks being overwritten. Using nmcli ties configuration to the connection lifecycle and avoids transient failures. Consider a case where DHCP updates DNS: the connection-level approach makes your desired DNS authoritative for that profile. Ask yourself: which interfaces in your fleet should carry corporate DNS versus public fallbacks?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DNS on RHEL and NetworkManager
Architecture: How DNS is applied
DNS settings belong to connection profiles. NetworkManager persists and applies them when an interface activates.
Why profiles win
Profiles prevent accidental overwrites from DHCP or restarts because DNS is tied to the interface configuration, not a single file edit.
Concrete example
Set dns4 to [192.168.1.1, 8.8.8.8] and dns4_search to [example.com] on the System eth0 profile to ensure consistent resolution for hosts on that interface.
Misconfiguration symptom
You see correct entries in /etc/resolv.conf but queries fail. Often the firewall or network path blocks DNS queries, not the file contents themselves.
nmcli via Ansible (visual walkthrough)
# example task
- name: Set DNS servers for the specified connection
  community.general.nmcli:
    conn_name: "{{ connection_name }}"
    dns4: "{{ dns_servers }}"
    dns4_search: "{{ dns_search_domains }}"
    state: present
This configuration attaches DNS to the connection name, applying the values persistently. Consider activating the connection after change to ensure immediate effect.

screens.title: Automate DNS with community.general.nmcli
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through an Ansible task that sets DNS on a connection profile. The pattern uses community. general. nmcli and supplies a connection name, a list of dns4 servers, and optional dns4_search domains. In practice you store values as variables at the top of your playbook: connection_name might be System eth0, and dns_servers might include 192.168.1.1 as a primary and 8.8.8.8 as a fallback. When you run the playbook the module ensures the connection exists and applies the DNS settings; NetworkManager then updates resolv. conf accordingly. A concrete example is shown in the visual code panel. Important operational notes: you can leave activate commented out because NetworkManager often applies changes dynamically, but explicitly activating the connection guarantees immediate application. After the task runs verify the result by first inspecting the file with cat /etc/resolv. conf, then run host or dig to confirm resolution of a known domain. A common mistake is misnaming the connection. If the connection_name does not match an existing profile, you may need to create or reference the correct profile. Closing takeaway: prefer connection-bound DNS entries so they survive reboots and DHCP updates; always verify with a live DNS query.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Automate DNS with nmcli
Task structure
Declare variables, call community.general.nmcli with conn_name, dns4, and dns4_search. Optionally activate the connection to apply immediately.
Operational notes
  • Ensure connection_name matches an existing profile.
  • Verify resolv.conf and run host or dig to test resolution.
  • Consider firewall rules if queries still fail.
Key Takeaway

Bind DNS to a connection profile to make settings persistent and suitable for automation across many hosts.

Example task (YAML)
---
- name: Configure DNS resolvers for a network connection
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes

  vars:
    connection_name: System eth0
    dns_servers:
      - 192.168.1.1
      - 8.8.8.8
    dns_search_domains:
      - example.com

  tasks:
    - name: Set DNS servers for the specified connection
      community.general.nmcli:
        conn_name: "{{ connection_name }}"
        dns4: "{{ dns_servers }}"
        dns4_search: "{{ dns_search_domains }}"
        state: present
After running, check resolv.conf and use a DNS query tool. If resolution fails, inspect firewall and network path for UDP 53 traffic.

screens.title: Verify DNS Resolution
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is about checking configuration and exercising it with real queries. Start by running cat /etc/resolv. conf to confirm the resolver IPs and search domains the OS is using. If the entries match your intended connection profile, run a query tool such as host or dig for a well-known domain like google. com. If you see no answer or timeouts, a frequent cause is a firewall blocking outgoing UDP port 53. In that case check firewalld rules or network ACLs. If resolv. conf shows correct servers but queries fail, confirm that the DNS servers themselves are reachable by using ping to their IPs or by running a packet capture. Another troubleshooting step is to explicitly activate the connection profile after changing DNS so NetworkManager applies it immediately. A common mistake is assuming a correct resolv. conf proves success; it shows intent, but a successful DNS query proves reachability and correct transport. Follow the sequence: inspect resolv. conf, test a query, inspect firewall and connectivity, then check logs. Closing reflection: when a service cannot reach a hostname, can you determine from these steps whether the failure is local configuration, network path, or remote DNS server health?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Verify DNS Resolution
Verification Steps
  1. Run cat /etc/resolv.conf to confirm configured servers and search domains.
  2. Run dig +short google.com or host google.com to test resolution.
  3. If queries time out, check firewall rules for outgoing UDP port 53 and network ACLs.
  4. Ping the DNS server IPs to confirm reachability, or capture traffic to see whether queries leave the host.
Remember: a correct resolv.conf is only the first step. A successful DNS query proves the server is reachable and responding.
Example troubleshooting scenario
You applied a connection profile with two DNS servers and resolv.conf shows them, but dig fails. Next, inspect firewalld for blocked outgoing UDP 53. If firewalld allows, try pinging the DNS server. If ping works but dig still times out, capture packets to confirm DNS queries are sent and responses received.
Common mistake

Assuming resolv.conf equality equals functional DNS. Always run a DNS query to confirm end-to-end visibility.

screens.title: chrony and NTP on RHEL
screens.narratorSegment: chrony is the NTP implementation recommended on modern RHEL releases. Unlike older daemons, chrony is designed to handle machines that are frequently offline or that have variable network latency, and it can converge on correct time quickly. The main configuration file is /etc/chrony. conf, where you specify server or pool directives pointing to NTP sources such as 0. rhel. pool. ntp. org or your internal ntp. example. com. In an automated workflow you deploy a template for this file using ansible. builtin. template, which allows you to propagate a consistent list of servers to many hosts. Once chrony is installed and configured, the chronyd service must be running and enabled. To check synchronization, use chronyc sources. Note that synchronization can take a few minutes after service start. Common misconfigurations include incorrect server names or blocked UDP port 123. For example, if chronyc sources shows no active sources despite chronyd running, check the chrony. conf entries for reachable servers and ensure the firewall does not block NTP traffic. The practical rule is to manage chrony configuration as code and verify synchronization with chronyc after deployment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › chrony and NTP on RHEL
What is chrony?
chrony is an NTP implementation that synchronizes system clocks reliably, even on systems with intermittent network connectivity.
Configuration
Define server or pool directives in /etc/chrony.conf, for example pool 0.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst, and deploy via ansible.builtin.template for consistency.
Verification
Run chronyc sources to confirm active NTP sources, and allow a few minutes after starting the service for synchronization to converge.
Troubleshooting
If chronyd runs but shows no sources, check chrony.conf entries and firewall rules blocking UDP 123.
chrony.conf template snippet
# Use public NTP servers from the pool project.
{% for server in ntp_servers %}
server {{ server }}
{% endfor %}

driftfile /var/lib/chrony/drift
rtcsync
logdir /var/log/chrony
Deploy this template with ansible.builtin.template, then notify a handler to restart chronyd so the new servers are used.

screens.title: Deploying chrony with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable deployment pattern installs chrony, templates /etc/chrony. conf, ensures chronyd is enabled, and verifies sources. In Ansible, install the package with ansible. builtin. package and use ansible. builtin. template to render chrony. conf. j2 with your ntp_servers variables. The template lets you iterate servers so each host receives identical configuration. Include a handler named Restart chronyd that calls systemd to restart the chronyd unit when the template changes. After the handler runs, ensure chronyd is enabled and started with ansible. builtin. systemd. To verify, run chronyc sources and inspect the output. The playbook example in the visual panel matches the chapter source and includes a handler. Practical tips: set file ownership and mode on the deployed file and include daemon_reload if systemd needs it after config changes. A common misconception is to assume chronyd synchronization is immediate; allow a few minutes for convergence. Finally, always check firewall settings for UDP 123 if chronyc shows no active sources despite correct configuration. Deploying chrony with Ansible means install chrony, deploy chrony.conf via template, restart chronyd via handler, enable service, then verify with chronyc sources.. In practical terms, playbook tasks, handlers, and template usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Deploying chrony with Ansible
Playbook flow
  • Install chrony package.
  • Deploy chrony.conf.j2 via ansible.builtin.template and set owner, group, mode.
  • Notify handler to restart chronyd.
  • Ensure chronyd service is enabled and started.
  • Verify with chronyc sources.
Remember to allow a few minutes for synchronization and to check firewall rules if no sources appear.
Playbook snippet
- name: Ensure chrony package is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: chrony
    state: present

- name: Deploy chrony.conf from template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: chrony.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/chrony.conf
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: '0644'
  notify: Restart chronyd

- name: Ensure chronyd service is running and enabled
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: chronyd
    state: started
    enabled: yes

handlers:
  - name: Restart chronyd
    ansible.builtin.systemd:
      name: chronyd
      state: restarted
      daemon_reload: yes

screens.title: Ensuring chronyd runs and recovers
screens.narratorSegment: Managing chronyd reliably means more than installing a package. Ensure the service is enabled so it starts after reboot, and start it immediately so synchronization begins. Use ansible. builtin. systemd with name chronyd, state started, and enabled yes. When the template for chrony. conf changes, notify a handler to restart the daemon and include daemon_reload if necessary. After the service is running, verification steps include checking unit status and running chronyc sources to see which servers are being used and which are synchronized. If chronyc shows servers but no active or synced sources, wait a few minutes for convergence and check network connectivity. If the service repeatedly fails to start, inspect journal logs for permission issues, malformed configuration directives, or missing driftfile paths. A common pitfall is missing file owner or wrong file mode on /etc/chrony. conf that prevents chronyd from reading it. Automate these checks in your playbooks by asserting file ownership and running a verification command that registers output so you can debug on failures. In the lab, practice running the handler and observing chronyc sources change state after a short interval.

- name: Verify NTP synchronization

screens.title: Common misconfigurations and impacts
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding common misconfigurations helps you detect and fix faults faster. For DNS, a frequent error is entering incorrect DNS server IPs in a connection profile or placing DNS entries only in /etc/resolv. conf so they are transient. The symptom will be correct file contents but failed queries; check firewall rules for UDP 53. Another DNS issue is forgetting to set dns4_search domains causing failed lookups for short hostnames. For NTP, common mistakes include wrong server names in chrony. conf, not enabling or starting chronyd, or firewall rules blocking UDP 123. The symptom there is chronyc sources showing no synchronized sources even though the service is running. In both cases a helpful troubleshooting sequence is: confirm configuration, run a live query or chronyc, then inspect the network path and firewall. Contrast the two: DNS failures typically manifest as inability to resolve names; NTP issues show as clock skew, authentication failures, or chronyc indicating no sources. A misconception is to treat these as low priority; in practice they can silently degrade authentication, logging accuracy and service interoperability. Closing question: after verifying configuration, which logs or packet-level checks would you run to isolate the problem further?

screens.title: Assessment and troubleshooting questions
screens.narratorSegment: Use assessment scenarios to sharpen diagnostic skills. Scenario one: after applying a DNS profile your resolv. conf contains the correct servers but dig google. com still fails. The most likely cause is a network or firewall issue blocking UDP 53. Confirm by checking firewalld rules and by pinging the DNS server IP. Scenario two: you deployed chrony. conf and chronyd is running, but chronyc sources shows no synchronized sources. First check that the server entries in chrony. conf are reachable and correct, then check firewall rules for UDP 123. Scenario three: you edited /etc/resolv. conf manually and later a DHCP client overwrote it. The root cause is not using NetworkManager profiles. As part of troubleshooting, always separate configuration intent from runtime evidence: configuration files show intent, while dig or chronyc output show runtime behavior. A common misconception is to assume a running service implies correct configuration; services can be running but misconfigured. Close by asking: given an observed failure, which verification command provides the most direct evidence for configuration correctness vs network reachability? fullNarratorScript:
In real systems, DNS and NTP are quietly foundational. DNS translates human names into network addresses so services can find each other, and NTP keeps system clocks aligned so logs, certificates, and authentication remain valid. In this lesson you will learn how to automate client-side DNS using NetworkManager via the community. general. nmcli Ansible module, and how to deploy and verify chrony as the NTP client via Ansible templates or targeted edits. You will see concrete playbook examples for setting DNS on a connection profile named System eth0, and for templating /etc/chrony. conf and ensuring chronyd is running. We also cover verification commands — cat /etc/resolv. conf, dig or host, and chronyc sources — plus common faults such as firewall blocking and incorrect server entries. By the end you will understand why tying DNS to a NetworkManager connection profile avoids transient overwritten settings, and why chrony is preferred on modern RHEL systems for fast, reliable synchronization. Consider how an incorrect DNS or unsynchronized clock could silently break updates or authentication on production systems; that risk is why we automate and verify these services.

Across these objectives you will learn to explain why DNS and NTP matter, automate DNS via NetworkManager, deploy chrony with Ansible templates, verify services, and find common misconfigurations. First, you'll describe how DNS resolution and time synchronization affect availability and security, with examples like failed package updates and certificate validation errors. Second, you'll automate client-side DNS by configuring a NetworkManager connection profile using the community. general. nmcli module so resolv. conf is managed predictably instead of being overwritten. Third, you'll deploy a chrony configuration using ansible. builtin. template or make targeted edits with lineinfile, install the chrony package, and ensure chronyd is enabled. Fourth, you will run verification commands and interpret results — for DNS use dig or host and inspect resolv. conf, for NTP use chronyc sources and service checks — and you will learn what an incorrect server entry or a firewall block looks like. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to anchor the skill and a verified competency milestone so you can self-check your work.

This second objectives slide gives you a concrete picture of success. For DNS automation, success means a NetworkManager connection profile such as System eth0 lists dns4 entries and dns4_search domains so /etc/resolv. conf contains the correct servers even after reboots. For chrony deployment, success means a templated /etc/chrony. conf delivered identically to all hosts, chrony package installed, chronyd enabled and started, and chronyc sources showing active NTP sources after a few minutes. Verification success includes reading resolv. conf, running dig or host to confirm name resolution, and using chronyc sources to confirm synchronization state. Troubleshooting success means you can infer whether a failure is a firewall block, incorrect server IP, or a service not started. A common misconception is thinking editing /etc/resolv. conf directly is persistent; in RHEL you should prefer configuring NetworkManager profiles so changes survive interface events. Use the verified competency milestones to test each outcome on a lab host.

Start by understanding the failure modes. DNS resolves human-friendly hostnames to IP addresses. If DNS fails, services that rely on names cannot connect and many automation tools break when they cannot reach package mirrors or A P I endpoints. A concrete example is a web server configured to reach a backend by hostname; if resolv. conf points to incorrect servers or network rules block DNS, the web server fails to reach the backend even though network connectivity may exist. NTP prevents clock drift. If a server's clock drifts, authentication protocols and certificate validity checks can fail. For example, Kerberos authentication and TLS certificate validation both depend on reasonably synchronized clocks. A practical contrast: editing /etc/resolv. conf manually can appear to work for a single session, but NetworkManager may overwrite the file when interfaces change. The recommended practice is to set DNS in the NetworkManager connection profile using community. general. nmcli so the setting persists and is associated with a named interface. For NTP, modern RHEL uses chrony instead of ntpd; deploy a templated chrony. conf so every host points to approved NTP sources. In short: persistent, automated configuration avoids intermittent failures and simplifies troubleshooting. Ask yourself: if a host cannot resolve names or has a wrong time, which user-facing services would fail first in your environment?

On RHEL systems NetworkManager commonly manages network interfaces and the contents of the file /etc/resolv. conf. That file lists the DNS servers and search domains the resolver uses. If you edit that file directly, NetworkManager or an interface event can overwrite your changes. The more robust pattern is to declare DNS servers on the NetworkManager connection profile itself so the DNS configuration is bound to an interface name like System eth0. The community. general. nmcli Ansible module lets you express connection-level DNS settings in a reproducible way. For example, set dns4 to a list such as 192.168.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 and set dns4_search to include example. com. When applied, NetworkManager updates its profile and applies the settings, which persist and survive reboots and reactivations. A common misconception is that using ansible. builtin. template on /etc/resolv. conf is sufficient; while possible, it risks being overwritten. Using nmcli ties configuration to the connection lifecycle and avoids transient failures. Consider a case where DHCP updates DNS: the connection-level approach makes your desired DNS authoritative for that profile. Ask yourself: which interfaces in your fleet should carry corporate DNS versus public fallbacks?

Let's walk through an Ansible task that sets DNS on a connection profile. The pattern uses community. general. nmcli and supplies a connection name, a list of dns4 servers, and optional dns4_search domains. In practice you store values as variables at the top of your playbook: connection_name might be System eth0, and dns_servers might include 192.168.1.1 as a primary and 8.8.8.8 as a fallback. When you run the playbook the module ensures the connection exists and applies the DNS settings; NetworkManager then updates resolv. conf accordingly. A concrete example is shown in the visual code panel. Important operational notes: you can leave activate commented out because NetworkManager often applies changes dynamically, but explicitly activating the connection guarantees immediate application. After the task runs verify the result by first inspecting the file with cat /etc/resolv. conf, then run host or dig to confirm resolution of a known domain. A common mistake is misnaming the connection. If the connection_name does not match an existing profile, you may need to create or reference the correct profile. Closing takeaway: prefer connection-bound DNS entries so they survive reboots and DHCP updates; always verify with a live DNS query.

Verification is about checking configuration and exercising it with real queries. Start by running cat /etc/resolv. conf to confirm the resolver IPs and search domains the OS is using. If the entries match your intended connection profile, run a query tool such as host or dig for a well-known domain like google. com. If you see no answer or timeouts, a frequent cause is a firewall blocking outgoing UDP port 53. In that case check firewalld rules or network ACLs. If resolv. conf shows correct servers but queries fail, confirm that the DNS servers themselves are reachable by using ping to their IPs or by running a packet capture. Another troubleshooting step is to explicitly activate the connection profile after changing DNS so NetworkManager applies it immediately. A common mistake is assuming a correct resolv. conf proves success; it shows intent, but a successful DNS query proves reachability and correct transport. Follow the sequence: inspect resolv. conf, test a query, inspect firewall and connectivity, then check logs. Closing reflection: when a service cannot reach a hostname, can you determine from these steps whether the failure is local configuration, network path, or remote DNS server health?

chrony is the NTP implementation recommended on modern RHEL releases. Unlike older daemons, chrony is designed to handle machines that are frequently offline or that have variable network latency, and it can converge on correct time quickly. The main configuration file is /etc/chrony. conf, where you specify server or pool directives pointing to NTP sources such as 0. rhel. pool. ntp. org or your internal ntp. example. com. In an automated workflow you deploy a template for this file using ansible. builtin. template, which allows you to propagate a consistent list of servers to many hosts. Once chrony is installed and configured, the chronyd service must be running and enabled. To check synchronization, use chronyc sources. Note that synchronization can take a few minutes after service start. Common misconfigurations include incorrect server names or blocked UDP port 123. For example, if chronyc sources shows no active sources despite chronyd running, check the chrony. conf entries for reachable servers and ensure the firewall does not block NTP traffic. The practical rule is to manage chrony configuration as code and verify synchronization with chronyc after deployment.

A repeatable deployment pattern installs chrony, templates /etc/chrony. conf, ensures chronyd is enabled, and verifies sources. In Ansible, install the package with ansible. builtin. package and use ansible. builtin. template to render chrony. conf. j2 with your ntp_servers variables. The template lets you iterate servers so each host receives identical configuration. Include a handler named Restart chronyd that calls systemd to restart the chronyd unit when the template changes. After the handler runs, ensure chronyd is enabled and started with ansible. builtin. systemd. To verify, run chronyc sources and inspect the output. The playbook example in the visual panel matches the chapter source and includes a handler. Practical tips: set file ownership and mode on the deployed file and include daemon_reload if systemd needs it after config changes. A common misconception is to assume chronyd synchronization is immediate; allow a few minutes for convergence. Finally, always check firewall settings for UDP 123 if chronyc shows no active sources despite correct configuration. Deploying chrony with Ansible means install chrony, deploy chrony.conf via template, restart chronyd via handler, enable service, then verify with chronyc sources.. In practical terms, playbook tasks, handlers, and template usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Managing chronyd reliably means more than installing a package. Ensure the service is enabled so it starts after reboot, and start it immediately so synchronization begins. Use ansible. builtin. systemd with name chronyd, state started, and enabled yes. Understanding common misconfigurations helps you detect and fix faults faster. For DNS, a frequent error is entering incorrect DNS server IPs in a connection profile or placing DNS entries only in /etc/resolv. conf so they are transient. The symptom will be correct file contents but failed queries; check firewall rules for UDP 53. Another DNS issue is forgetting to set dns4_search domains causing failed lookups for short hostnames. For NTP, common mistakes include wrong server names in chrony. conf, not enabling or starting chronyd, or firewall rules blocking UDP 123. The symptom there is chronyc sources showing no synchronized sources even though the service is running. In both cases a helpful troubleshooting sequence is: confirm configuration, run a live query or chronyc, then inspect the network path and firewall. Contrast the two: DNS failures typically manifest as inability to resolve names; NTP issues show as clock skew, authentication failures, or chronyc indicating no sources. A misconception is to treat these as low priority; in practice they can silently degrade authentication, logging accuracy and service interoperability. These three concise concepts summarize what you should remember. First, DNS is the mapping system that allows services to find each other by name; configure DNS persistently by setting values on NetworkManager connection profiles rather than editing the resolver file directly. Second, chrony is the recommended NTP implementation on modern RHEL systems; deploy a templated /etc/chrony. conf, ensure chronyd is enabled and started, and verify synchronization with chronyc sources. Third, verification and troubleshooting follow a simple pattern: inspect configuration files to confirm intent, run live queries to measure runtime behavior, and then check network and firewall rules when results do not match intent. Together these ideas help you automate robust environments where name resolution and timekeeping do not become intermittent failure modes.
